thread.title: Here's Why You Should Not Sell Stocks

author: Stephen McBride
title: Here's Why You Should Not Sell Stocks
text:
“Stocks are plunging… what should I do?” That’s the #1 question I’m asked after the recent S&P 500 sell-off.
I can tell folks are nervous. I understand why. This has been no run-of-the-mill dip for stocks.
By one widely followed measure of market momentum, stocks briefly entered a freefall that was worse than anything we’ve seen since 1990! But journalists are serving up a big dose of fear, too.
CNBC held a special six-hour-long Markets in Turmoil segment. All the big networks broke out their scary red BREAKING NEWS banners.
If you’ve been reading me, you know that I urge you to ignore these so-called “experts.” That’s especially true if you are invested in what I call “disruptor stocks.” These are technology companies like Amazon or NVIDIA that are shaping the future.
Let me explain.
Stocks that Hand You Life-Changing Gains Are Prone to Volatility—Deal with It Take Amazon (AMZN), for example. The company in effect invented the online marketplace. It has handed early investors 22,000% gains and counting.
And Apple’s (AAPL) iPhone is the main reason why 85% of Americans carry a smartphone. Its stock has rocketed 14,000% since 2004.
These results show you can make life-changing gains by investing in the right “disruptor stock” … at the right time. But owning these businesses is not a one-way road to riches.
These stocks attract a lot of excitement from investors. Which makes their stocks prone to big moves both UP and DOWN.
Amazon Has Shot Up 400% Since It Was Deemed Dead in 2014 Amazon took shareholders for a roller coaster ride in 2014. The stock plunged 30%, which prompted the media to run stories like…
“Is Amazon Going Through an Identity Crisis? ”
“Amazon to $100?”
The stock is up over 400% since then… and trades at around $1,650 today.
It’s the same story for big, disruptive stocks like Google (GOOG), Microsoft (MSFT), and dozens of others . They all suffer through bad weeks and months.
But investors who’ve stayed the course have made 10x gains or bigger.
A Correction Is the Market’s Way of Testing You I spend all of my professional time on the hunt for disruptive businesses with the potential to hand us triple-digit profits . But finding these stocks is only half the battle.
Once you buy a stock, your biggest challenge is to own it through the bumps and dips which the market will serve up.
It’s not easy to hold on when markets look wobbly like they do right now. You’ll want to hit the sell button when you see nothing but red charts on the screen.
But let me tell you something…
US Stocks Haven’t Had a Losing Year Since 2008 The S&P 500 has surged almost 300% in the past nine years. But it has not been “smooth sailing.” In the past nine years, the S&P has dropped 19%, 16%, 13%, and 10% five separate times.
These corrections were nothing to panic over. In fact, pullbacks suggest that investors are acting cautiously.
This is a good thing for the market’s longer-term health. It’s when the market goes straight up every day that you should be worried.
Remember in January when stocks were on a tear? Investors cheered as the S&P soared 8% in the first 26 days.
That euphoria concerns me far more than any correction. Case in point: The market peaked on January 26. In just a few days, it plunged 10%, erasing all its 2018 gains.
Why a 20%+ Drop in Stocks Is Unlikely in the Near Future A reliable way to check the market’s “pulse” is by examining the economy. Most crashes in US stocks have happened while the US economy was shrinking.
Since the 1920s, we’ve had 10 bear markets in US stocks. Eight of the 10 have come inside a recession.
The ninth was during the Cuban missile crisis. And the tenth was “Black Monday” 1987, when stocks plunged 23% in a single day. You could consider both black swan events.
These non-recession bear markets on average lasted less than six months and fell an average of 31%. The bear markets that occurred during recessions lasted two-and-a-half years and fell 49%, on average.
Drilling down further: When the S&P 500 falls 10% or more while the economy is growing , stocks rise 24% on average the following year.
U nless the Economy Tanks, I Won’t Sell Stocks How is the economy looking today?
In a word, great. Most of the indicators I monitor say the US economy is healthy as an ox. I’ll give you one example: the unemployment rate.
My research shows the unemployment rate began to rise about 12 months before each recession in the past 60 years. Essentially, it has warned us of every single recession for the past six decades… roughly a year in advance.
Unemployment in the US today is 3.7%, which is almost a 50-year low. This indicator, along with several others, continues to give me the "green light" for owning stocks today.
